segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One day, as he was teaching the people in the temple and announcing the good news, the chief priests and the scribes came up with the elders

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Tell us by what authority you are doing these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I will also ask you a question, and you tell me:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The baptism of John—was it from heaven or from human beings?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They discussed it among themselves, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But if we say, ‘From human beings,’ all the people will stone us, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they answered that they did not know where it was from.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Neither am I telling you by what authority I am doing these things.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he began to tell the people this parable:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “A man planted a vineyard, leased it to tenants, and went abroad for a long time.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When the season came, he sent a slave to the tenants so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He went on to send another slave; but that one too they beat and treated shamefully and sent away empty-handed.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He went on to send a third; this one too they wounded and threw out.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But when the tenants saw him, they reasoned with one another, saying, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance will be ours.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard this, they said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “May it never happen!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he looked straight at them and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What then is this that is written: ‘The stone that the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Everyone who falls on that stone will be shattered, and it will crush anyone on whom it falls.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, but they feared the people; for they realized that he had told this parable against them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they watched him closely and sent spies who pretended to be righteous, so that they might catch him in something he said and so hand him over to the jurisdiction and authority of the governor.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They questioned him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly and show no partiality, but teach the way of God in truth.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Are we permitted to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he saw through their craftiness and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Show me a denarius. Whose image and inscription does it have?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Caesar’s.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Then give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they were not able to catch him in what he said in front of the people; and marveling at his answer, they fell silent.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some of the Sadducees, who deny that there is a resurrection, came up and questioned him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies leaving a wife but no children, the man should take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife and died childless;

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: then the second

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and the third took her; and in the same way all seven left no children and died.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Finally the woman died too.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So in the resurrection, whose wife does the woman become? For all seven had her as wife.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but those who are counted worthy to attain that age and the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels, and they are children of God, being children of the resurrection.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But that the dead are raised, even Moses made known in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord ‘the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He is not God of the dead but of the living, for to him all are alive.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then some of the scribes answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, you have spoken well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For they no longer dared to ask him anything.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How can they say that the Messiah is David’s son?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For David himself says in the book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord: “Sit at my right hand

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: David, then, calls him ‘Lord’; so how is he his son?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While all the people were listening, he said to the disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: who devour widows’ houses and for show pray at length. These will receive a harsher judgment.”

notes.note: The Greek verb was an ordinary word for bringing or publicly announcing good news. “Gospel” has since become a religious term and the name of a kind of book, so “good news” is closer to what a first-century hearer understood. Many modern translations make the same choice.

The Greek word names a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. Most older English versions say “servant”; several modern ones use “slave” here. The owner’s right to send these men and the tenants’ contempt for them both fit that status.

The quotation is from Psalm 118:22. The Greek is literally “head of the corner,” which may mean a foundation stone at the corner of a building or the stone that crowns it, such as a capstone or keystone. Scholars are divided; either way it is the most important stone in the structure.

The verb ordinarily means “winnow,” and from that “scatter like chaff.” Most lexicons and translations take it here as “crush,” in line with the image of a falling stone and with a Greek version of Daniel 2:44, where the same verb is used of a kingdom that shatters all others. “Scatter him like chaff” is a possible alternative.

This is the ordinary Greek verb for transferring someone into another’s custody or power. The Gospels use the same word for what Judas, the priests and Pilate each do to Jesus, and this translation renders it “hand over” throughout so that the chain is visible.

notes.phrase: Are we permitted to pay tribute
notes.traditional: Is it lawful for us to give tribute
notes.note: The question is whether God’s law allows it, not whether Roman law does; “lawful” can suggest the latter to a modern reader. The word for “tribute” denotes the tax a subject people paid to its foreign ruler, which was a standing grievance in Judea. A yes would discredit Jesus with the people, and a no would be grounds for a charge before the governor.

A Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s wage for a laborer. Those of the reigning emperor Tiberius carried his portrait and an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus. Jesus’ questioners can produce one even though they are in the temple.

The questioners asked about “giving” tribute, but Jesus answers with a stronger verb that means to pay what is owed or return what belongs to someone. “Give back” keeps that shift; many modern versions have simply “give.”

notes.phrase: raise up offspring for his brother
notes.traditional: raise up seed unto his brother
notes.note: The reference is to the law of levirate marriage in Deuteronomy 25:5–6. When a married man died without a son, his brother was to marry the widow, and the first son born counted as the dead man’s heir. The Sadducees, who accepted no resurrection, use this law to build a case meant to make the idea look absurd.

The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era, not the physical world. Jesus is using the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come. “Children of” (literally “sons of”) is a Semitic idiom for those who belong to something, and it recurs in verse 36. Most modern translations also have “age” here.

notes.phrase: in the passage about the bush
notes.note: The Greek says only “at the bush.” Before chapter and verse numbers existed, a passage of Scripture was cited by a key word; this one is the burning bush account in Exodus 3. Jesus argues from the books of Moses because the Sadducees gave them the highest authority.

The Greek word here is a title, “the anointed one,” for the king Israel expected, and the question is about that figure’s descent. “Messiah” conveys the title; “Christ” now sounds like a name. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

notes.phrase: The Lord said to my Lord
notes.traditional: The LORD said unto my Lord
notes.note: The quotation is Psalm 110:1. In Greek the same word, “lord,” appears twice; in the Hebrew the first is the divine name and the second is the ordinary word for a master or superior. Jesus’ argument turns on the second: David, the supposed author, calls the coming king his own lord.
